nameStory: The "stinking" in stinking chamomile comes from its notoriously unpleasant odor that hits you when you crush the leaves or flowers. Unlike true chamomile with its sweet, apple-like scent, this plant smells downright foul - earning it colorful nicknames like "pig-sty-daisy" and "dog-fennel." The name "cotula" comes from the Greek word for "small cup," describing the cup-like shape of its flower centers.
description: Stinking chamomile is a weedy annual flower that looks deceptively pretty from a distance with its white daisy-like blooms and feathery green leaves. This European immigrant grows 1-2 feet tall with branching stems and finely divided, almost lacy foliage. Don't let its innocent appearance fool you - this is one wildflower that announces itself with a memorable stench when disturbed. It spreads readily in disturbed soils and can form substantial patches in fields and roadsides.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: The most reliable identifier - crush a leaf or flower and you'll get a distinctly unpleasant, acrid odor that's nothing like sweet chamomile

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white daisy-like flowers about 3/4 inch across with yellow centers and white petals that often curve backward, giving a slightly raggedy appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, feathery leaves that are finely cut into thread-like segments, feeling somewhat sticky and rough to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy, much-branched annual that grows 1-2 feet tall with multiple flower heads clustered at the ends of branches

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, green stems that branch frequently and feel slightly sticky when handled, often with a reddish tinge

habitat: Look for stinking chamomile in disturbed areas like roadsides, field edges, vacant lots, and farmland throughout New England. It thrives in poor, compacted soils and sunny locations where other plants struggle. You'll often find it mixed with other weedy species in areas that have been recently disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with feathery leaves, already developing their characteristic unpleasant smell when crushed.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with numerous small white daisy flowers covering the bushy plants from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline and set seed, with dried flower heads persisting into early fall before the annual plants die.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain as this is an annual plant, but seeds lie dormant in the soil ready for next year's germination.

funFact: This plant's terrible smell is actually a chemical defense system - it produces compounds so offensive that even hungry livestock usually avoid eating it, giving it a competitive advantage in overgrazed pastures where more palatable plants get munched down to nothing.
confusionNotes: Easily confused with true chamomile (German chamomile), but the smell test is foolproof - true chamomile smells sweetly of apples when crushed, while stinking chamomile reeks. Memory trick: if it smells good enough to make tea with, it's true chamomile; if it makes you wrinkle your nose, it's the stinking kind.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "chamomile," this plant is not used medicinally like true German chamomile - in fact, it can cause skin irritation and blisters in sensitive people. The name confusion has led to some unfortunate mix-ups by foragers, making the smell test absolutely crucial for anyone interested in wild plants.
compareHints: Stinking chamomile is the only Anthemis species commonly found in New England, but it can be distinguished from other white-flowered members of the daisy family by its extremely finely divided, almost thread-like leaves and distinctive foul odor. Most other daisy-family weeds like ox-eye daisy have broader, less divided leaves and lack the offensive smell.
